content: Sulfur, also spelled sulphur in some regions, is a chemical element represented by the symbol S and atomic number 16. It is a non-metal that is abundant, tasteless, and multivalent. In its natural state, sulfur appears as a yellow crystalline solid. It can be found in its pure elemental form or as part of sulfide and sulfate minerals. Sulfur is essential for life, as it is a component of the amino acids cysteine and methionine. Commercially, sulfur is primarily used in fertilizers, but it also has applications in gunpowder, matches, insecticides, and fungicides. Brightly colored sulfur crystals are often sought after by mineral collectors due to their polyhedral shapes. Historically, sulfur has been known since ancient times. It is mentioned in Sanskrit texts as sulvari and in Latin as sulfur or sulphur. In English translations of the Bible, sulfur was referred to as brimstone, which contributed to the term fire and brimstone in sermons warning of eternal damnation. Despite its association with the smell of Hell, elemental sulfur is actually odorless. The smell often linked to sulfur comes from compounds like hydrogen sulfide (rotten eggs) or burning sulfur, which produces sulfur dioxide. Sulfur was known in China as early as the 6th century BC, where it was called brimstone or shiliuhuang. By the 3rd century, the Chinese discovered how to extract sulfur from pyrite. Early uses of sulfur included its flammability and reactivity with metals, as well as its role in traditional Chinese medicine. By 1044 AD, sulfur was a key component in Chinese gunpowder, a mixture of potassium nitrate, carbon, and sulfur. Alchemists assigned sulfur its own symbol, a triangle atop a cross. In the late 18th century, Antoine Lavoisier demonstrated that sulfur is an element, not a compound. In 1867, sulfur deposits were discovered in Louisiana and Texas, leading to the development of the Frasch process for extraction. The spelling of sulfur has varied historically. In the UK, Ireland, and other Commonwealth countries, sulphur was traditionally used, while sulfur is the standard in the United States. Both spellings are used in Australia, New Zealand, and Canada. The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) adopted sulfur in 1990, and this spelling has become increasingly uniform in scientific and non-official texts. Sulfur has several isotopes, with 35S being the only long-lived radioactive isotope, formed by cosmic ray spallation of argon-40 in the atmosphere. It has a half-life of 87 days. Isotopic differences in sulfur compounds can provide insights into geological and environmental processes, such as ore formation and pollution sources. Sulfur exists in more than 30 solid allotropes, more than any other element. The most common form is the cyclic S8 molecule, but other rings like S7 and S6 also exist. Larger rings, such as S12 and S18, have been synthesized. Sulfur's molten state exhibits unusual viscosity behavior, increasing above 200°C due to polymer formation. Rapid cooling of molten sulfur produces amorphous or plastic sulfur, which is metastable and reverts to crystalline form over time. Elemental sulfur is found near hot springs and volcanic regions, particularly along the Pacific Ring of Fire. It is mined in places like Indonesia, Chile, and Japan. Significant deposits also exist in salt domes along the Gulf of Mexico and in evaporites in Eastern Europe and Western Asia. These deposits are often formed by anaerobic bacteria acting on sulfate minerals like gypsum, though geological processes can also produce native sulfur. Fossil-based sulfur deposits are a major source of commercial sulfur production in countries like the United States, Poland, and Russia. The hydrotreating of oil and gas has led to a surplus of sulfur, with large stockpiles in Alberta, Canada. Sulfur compounds are diverse and include sulfides, sulfites, and sulfates. Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) is known for its rotten egg smell and reacts with metals to form metal sulfides like pyrite (iron sulfide), also known as fool's gold. Organic sulfur compounds, such as mercaptans, contribute to the odors of garlic and skunk spray. Some, like grapefruit mercaptan, have pleasant scents. Sulfur compounds also have industrial applications, such as in vulcanization of rubber, production of sulfuric acid, and as preservatives in dried fruits. Biologically, sulfur is essential for all living cells. It is absorbed by plants as sulfate and reduced to sulfide before being incorporated into amino acids like cysteine and methionine. Sulfur-containing compounds like glutathione play critical roles in cellular redox reactions. Disulfide bonds between cysteine residues contribute to the structural integrity of proteins, such as in hair and feathers. In traditional medicine, elemental sulfur has been used in creams to treat skin conditions like psoriasis, eczema, and acne. Its mechanism of action is not fully understood but may involve mild antibacterial and reducing properties. Environmentally, sulfur dioxide (SO2) from burning fossil fuels reacts with water and oxygen to form sulfuric acid, a major component of acid rain. This lowers the pH of soil and water, causing ecological damage and weathering of structures. Regulations now require sulfur to be removed from fuels to mitigate acid rain formation. Precautions are necessary when handling sulfur compounds like hydrogen sulfide and sulfur dioxide, as they can be toxic and harmful to tissues. Hydrogen sulfide, in particular, is dangerous because it quickly deadens the sense of smell, making it difficult to detect at lethal concentrations.
